claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution.
Components inside a Pulumi package inherit the package's version.

Pulumi recommends strategies for structuring Git repositories used to publish packages, and following them improves reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed of packages an organization builds and consumes.
See the Pulumi packages concept page at /docs/iac/concepts/packages/ and the components concept page at /docs/iac/concepts/components/ exist.
Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
A source-based plugin package is distributed as source code in a Git repository.
A source-based package's version is the Git tag on its repository.
Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow, typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.

The Pulumi IDP Private Registry exists as a concept page at /docs/idp/concepts/private-registry/ and the packaging-components guide anchors (#source-based-plugin-packages, #executable-based-plugin-packages) exist.
Publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry requires applying a semver Git tag (e.g., v1.2.3) to the repository.
`pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
The `pulumi package publish` step often runs automated tests before publishing.
The CLI command reference page /docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish/ exists for `pulumi package publish`.
Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
An executable-based package's version is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type; this is Pulumi's recommended practice.
A repository containing multiple Pulumi packages either has to release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are fine and expected, and the components ship together at the package's version.
Pulumi recommends defining exactly one package per repository, grouping a cohesive set of components in that package, and using multiple repositories (one per package) for distinct packages.

The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry (https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/eks/) bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
The components in the Pulumi Amazon EKS package are almost always used together and tend to evolve together.
A single `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repository root defines a Pulumi package, with components living alongside it.
The example repository layout places `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repo root with components under a `components/` directory (EksCluster, EksIam).
Bundling all of an organization's components into one giant monorepo package forfeits meaningful semantic versioning, and Pulumi does not recommend this approach.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
In the example, an enhancement to ComponentA releases the package at v1.1.0 (minor bump from v1.0.0), and a breaking change to ComponentB releases the package at v2.0.0 (major bump), per semver.
The Publishing packages guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/publishing-packages/.
